<iteration>3</iteration>

<reflection>
The high catalyst experiment provides strong discrimination. Best fits are now M5, M4, M3 (NLL ~-44 to -45), with M16, M11, M14, M20 moderately good. Pure MM (M1) and many deactivation variants fit poorly. M5 (two-step with catP intermediate), M4 (bifunctional catalyst X), and M3 (catalyst dimer activity) lead. Notably, models with substrate-induced inhibition (M11, M16) and catS deactivation (M14, M20) also perform well. M19 got much worse - cat+catS inactivation is unlikely. The aim of discriminating mechanisms was achieved.
</reflection>

<hypothesis>
The leading mechanisms differ in key ways:
- M5: catS+cat → catP+cat (two catalyst molecules needed) — second-order in cat
- M4: Separate species X converts S→P via catS
- M3: Dimeric cat2 is active form
- M11/M16: Substrate-induced catalyst deactivation
- M14/M20: CatS-based deactivation

To distinguish: an experiment with LOW catalyst and LOW substrate would test second-order cat dependence (M5, M3 would slow dramatically vs. M1-like). Alternatively, running with added product tests product inhibition (M12, M17) and product-dependent pathways. Running with high substrate tests substrate-induced deactivation (M11, M16).

The most diagnostic next test: low catalyst (0.001 M), moderate substrate (1.0 M). This:
- Dramatically slows M5 (needs catS+cat) and M3 (needs cat2) — rate ~[cat]²
- Normal MM-like rate for M1, M4 (M4 has X as separate species)
- Reduces deactivation effects (M9, M11, M14, M20) so should approach simple behavior
- Distinguishes order in catalyst
</hypothesis>
